title: Local Clifford equivalence to CSS codes: Polynomial-time classification and conversion
abstract: Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes support decoding and fault-tolerant logical operations through separate pure $X$ and pure $Z$ stabilizer checks. Generator choices and single-qubit Clifford transformations can obscure this structure. We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary stabilizer code is locally Clifford-equivalent to a CSS code and constructs the required transformation and CSS checks whenever such a form exists. For $m$ possibly redundant generator rows on $n$ qubits, the algorithm uses $O(mn^2+n^4)$ binary field operations. We reduce the problem to affine linear systems by characterizing local projectors that preserve the span of the binary stabilizer labels. The conversion preserves code parameters and check sparsity for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. We demonstrate CSS recovery and decoder reuse and resolve previously open LC-to-CSS classification questions for published code constructions. For graph states, LC-to-CSS equivalence corresponds to the existence of a bipartite graph in the local-complementation orbit. We derive a necessary-and-sufficient adjacency-matrix criterion for this property and construct such a graph whenever one exists. Our algorithm makes CSS decoding and fault-tolerant constructions accessible throughout the local Clifford equivalence classes of CSS codes.
summary: This paper introduces a deterministic, polynomial-time algorithm to classify whether any given stabilizer code can be transformed into a structured CSS code via local Clifford operations. By reducing the problem to solving affine linear systems, the authors provide a complete framework for constructing the necessary transformations and the pure X and Z stabilizer checks. This advances the theoretical understanding of code structure and fault-tolerance in quantum computing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the algorithmic problem of determining if an arbitrary stabilizer code is locally Clifford-equivalent (LC-equivalent) to a structured Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) code.
main_result: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is provided to decide this equivalence and, if true, construct the necessary single-qubit Clifford transformations and the pure X and Z stabilizer checks.
method: The problem is reduced to checking the consistency of affine linear systems derived from local projector conditions, utilizing binary linear algebra over F_2.
model_or_system: The study focuses on stabilizer codes, which are fundamental structures used in quantum error correction (QEC). CSS codes are a specific, structured subset of these codes that facilitate fault-tolerant operations.
key_observables: The binary Pauli labels of the stabilizer generators, the existence of local projectors, and the resulting pure X and pure Z check matrices ($H_X, H_Z$).
important_parameters: The complexity is bounded by $O(mn^2 + n^4)$ binary field operations for $m$ generators on $n$ qubits.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the problem can be decomposed into checking consistency across independent components of the stabilizer structure.
figures_summary: The notes reference Lemma 2 characterizing the projector, Proposition 3 detailing the two-branch reduction, and Algorithm 1 providing the full pseudo-code for the decision and conversion process.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the mathematical characterization of LC-to-CSS equivalence, reduces it to solving affine linear systems, and presents a comprehensive algorithm for both decision and construction, including specific results for graph states.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general algorithmic tool for classifying and simplifying quantum error-correcting codes, which is foundational knowledge for anyone working on fault-tolerant quantum computation.
